s05.slug: WEDNESDAY · 10:14 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: The laundry room is under everything: a long low room in the basement that smells of hot lint and dryer sheets and the sweet chemical bloom of other people’s detergent. Eight washers down one wall, three of them working. Six dryers down the other, and when one finishes it doesn’t chime, it buzzes, a flat mean blat like the wrong answer on a game show. In the corner, an upright piano with a dead F, which nobody in Delgado admits to playing and somebody plays, badly, at three in the morning.

body.title: Taped to Washer 1
body.text:
LAUNDRY ROOM HOURS
7 A.M.–11 P.M.
(THIS MEANS YOU.)
—P. Raman, RA

body: Jack has the long folding table and the fluorescent tube over it, which ticks. Upstairs Theo is cutting the wake with the sound up, and Washer 3 has his work flannels and the jeans that smell like the Hobart. On the table: the Hopkins, open; two Pink Pearls; a gray drift of crumbs; Hale’s Housman, foxed and clean; Hale’s Williams; a padded mailer with TRUMBULL on it in his block capitals. Every pencil mark he has made in this book since junior year at Mooney comes out tonight: *who talks like this* beside the Deutschland, *yes* beside the grandeur of God, a long argument with “Spring and Fall” he is a little sorry to lose and a little more sorry he wrote.

At 10:14 Lena is in the doorway with a basket on each hip. One is hers. The other is all white — Laney’s pledge whites, because Pi Lam wants white for something on Friday that nobody will explain to Laney — and for half a second, seeing him, Lena stops.
“Hi.”
“Hi.”

She takes the washers at the far end. She’s in her last clean things, a long-sleeved gray T-shirt with SACRED HEART DEBATE across the back, a cotton skirt, the Justins, her hair twisted up and stuck through with a pencil, and she sorts Laney’s whites from her own at a speed that says she grew up in a house where somebody always had to. Then she stands at the end of the dryers with her arms folded, and he stays at the table, and the room is very well lit.

They do the news. Samoa on the Fishbowl TV yesterday, the palms going under. Padang this morning, a hotel folded down on itself. “Two in two days,” she says. He says it is. That one dies. They do Laney: a white dress, white shoes and a can opener, Friday, reasons withheld. “A can opener.” “She asked me if it should be white.” That one almost lives. Then it dies too. They do the Jets on Sunday. “Sanchez is a rookie.” “He is.”
“How’s Becca?”
“Great. How’s Wes?”
“Great.”
Washer 6 thumps into its spin.
“Nine days,” Lena says.
“Nine days.”

She always reads his margins. Upside down across Hale’s table, over his shoulder, out of his back pocket without asking. Tonight the Hopkins lies open on the folding table with his pencil all over both pages, and she keeps her eyes on the dryer windows and Laney’s whites going round, as if the book belonged to some other guy who stepped out.

When he heaves his basket up onto the table to make room, the index card slides out of it and lands face up by her boot. His mother’s handwriting, Nonna’s dictation, underlined twice: *Whites in HOT. Darks in COLD. MEDALS OFF.* Lena picks it up. She reads it. Her mouth goes — he sees it start at the corner — and she gets it back.
“That’s good advice,” she says, and sets the card on top of his basket, squared to the edge.

So he tells her what he’s doing, because somebody has to say something that isn’t the news. The Hopkins goes to Trumbull tomorrow; Driftwood mails it as the seller, the only way a book gets in. With a Housman. “Hale gave me that one. For Danny.”
She looks over at the little foxed book. “Hale did.”
“No margins. He said they’d only erase them.”
She knows the rule. He told her on a pier. She looks at the Hopkins, and the gray crumbs, and the clock over the vending machine, and then she comes up the table and takes his spare Pink Pearl.
“Friends help,” Lena says.

The old Penguin is broken-backed enough to lie open anywhere. It lies across the table with its front half under his hand and its back half under hers, and they go at it from both ends: he has the early poems; she starts at the very back, in the letters and sermons, where his pencil got argumentative, and rubs out *says you* without slowing down. At a quarter to eleven she moves her wash to the dryers. Eleven comes and goes on the vending machine, and the building sleeps on over their heads.

Toward midnight she’s in the last sonnets, the ones he has read soft. He knows the page before she gets to it. She turns the leaf, and there it is under her hand — *Thou art indeed just, Lord, if I contend / With thee* — and beside it, small, in his pencil, from a night in September: *Show Lena.*
She doesn’t stop. She doesn’t look up. She erases it, three short strokes and a fourth to be sure, and bends down and blows the crumbs off the page.
“There,” she says. “He can have it.”

Danny’s first letter has lived inside the Hopkins since the weekend it came. Jack moves it into Hale’s Williams and closes the Williams on it. The vending machine says 11:50. The laminate on Washer 1 says they have been breaking a rule for fifty minutes.

response: “Thank you,” he says.
“It’s for Danny,” Lena says, and turns the page, and goes on. They erase in the dryers’ noise, the front of the book and the back of it, until the vending machine says 11:59.

choices.text: “You didn’t have to do that one.”
response: “You didn’t have to do that one.”
“Yes I did.” She takes the next margin out as if it were a stain. Then the dryers have the room again, and they erase in the noise, front and back, until the vending machine says 11:59.

choices.text: “Hopkins burned every poem he had when he went Jesuit. He’d call this a half measure.”
response: “Hopkins burned every poem he had when he went Jesuit,” Jack says. “He’d call this a half measure.”

Lena smiles at it, a nice smile, the kind you’d give a stranger’s toast at a wedding, and blows the crumbs off a page. They erase in the dryers’ noise, front and back, until the vending machine says 11:59.

They erase side by side. The crumbs pile up gray in the gutter of the book where the two halves meet, and down the row a dryer buzzes, long and flat, and nobody gets up. They erase in the noise until the vending machine says 11:59.

s05b.slug: THURSDAY · 12:00 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: At midnight her phone goes off on top of Dryer 4. Not a ring: an alarm, a small brave chime climbing a scale over and over, and the LG buzzes across the hot enamel on vibrate. Lena catches it at the edge, opens it, silences it, shuts it.
“It’s my feast,” she says, to the dryers.

He waits. She gives him a little more, and no more than this. Her grandmother said the Little Flower’s prayer at midnight on the first of October every year of Lena’s life, standing up at the kitchen counter with the radio off, and everybody in that house had better be asleep or praying. “Grandmère,” she says. Jack knows where Grandmère is: in the good dress, since the November after the storm. Lena turns the phone over in her hand. “So I set an alarm.”

Then, because she has never once been able to leave a fact on the table: “She died tonight. Thérèse. Well — in 1897. About seven in the evening. So it starts at midnight.” And: “Everybody in my family’s Thérèse something. Tess got it first. I got it second.”

The book is in his back pocket. It has been there since Tuesday at two, when he walked out of Driftwood with it, through a shift and a seminar and every hour of tonight, and he has still not decided whether a friend is allowed to give it to her.

choices.key: At midnight on her feast you gave Lena a secondhand *Story of a Soul* with your margins in it.
response: “Happy feast day,” he says, and takes it out of his pocket, and holds it out across the folding table: *Story of a Soul*, a white paperback gone soft at the corners, Thérèse on the cover in her veil.
Lena looks at the cover a good while before she takes it. Then she has it in her hands.

choices.text: “It’s used. Three dollars. Somebody highlighted the first part.”
choices.key: At midnight on her feast you gave Lena a three-dollar *Story of a Soul* with your margins in it.
response: He takes it out of his back pocket and slides it across. “It’s used. Three dollars. Somebody highlighted the first part.”
“You’re supposed to take the price off,” she says, already holding it. The $3 is still penciled inside the cover in the Driftwood owner’s hand, and she has both thumbs on it.

choices.key: At midnight on her feast you gave Lena a secondhand *Story of a Soul*. “Happy feast day, Magdalena Thérèse.”
response: He takes it out of his pocket and holds it out. “Happy feast day, Magdalena Thérèse.”
He has said *Magdalena* to her twice before, both times at the end of a night, saying goodnight. This is the first time with both names, on her saint’s day, in a basement, with a book in his hand.
She doesn’t answer. The dryers go round. Then she takes the book.

choices.text: Slide it down the folding table without a word.
choices.key: At midnight on her feast you slid a secondhand *Story of a Soul* down the laundry-room table to Lena. Your margins were in it.
response: He takes it out of his pocket and sends it down the folding table without a word. It skates through the eraser crumbs and stops against her basket.
Lena looks at it. She looks at him. Then she picks it up.

s05c.slug: THURSDAY · 12:02 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM

body.text: She hasn’t said anything about the name. She is holding the book close, the way she took it, as if somebody might ask for it back.

body: She opens it. The cover first: ICS Publications, the price in pencil. Then the highlighter, somebody’s yellow, faithful for forty pages and then quitting halfway through a sentence, as if the owner lost the pen or the faith. Then the margins. His pencil, small and slanting, all the way through. She turns a page, and another. She goes back. She looks at him over the top of it.
“You wrote in it,” Lena says. “You *wrote in it*, Costigan.”
He reaches for the Pink Pearl.

“Don’t you dare.” She pulls the book against her chest with both arms and turns half away with it, as if he might come over the table. Then she opens it again and reads him his own margins out loud, and the night turns over.

She finds the elevator first. Thérèse in the last manuscript, wanting to be a saint and knowing she’s too small for it: *“I am too little to climb the rough stairway of perfection… The elevator which must raise me up to heaven is Your arms, O Jesus!”* And beside it, in his pencil: *Easy for you.*
“*Easy for you*,” Lena reads, in his voice, flat as a parking lot in Ohio.

She pages back into the childhood. Léonie, too old for dolls, holding out a basket of doll clothes to her little sisters: *choose*. Céline takes a ball of wool. Thérèse, who is four, says *I choose all!* and takes the basket. Beside it: *NO.*
“No *what*?” Lena says. “She’s describing her *sister*. Léonie’s giving away her dolls.”
“Thérèse took the whole basket.”
“She was *four*.”
“She says it’s the story of her life.”

“It *is* the story of her life, that’s the *point* — ” and she’s already gone on, to Thérèse saying Jesus has no need of books or teachers to instruct a soul, and his pencil beside it: *She’d have hated Hale.*
“She’d have *prayed* for Hale,” Lena says. “She prayed a murderer onto a crucifix at fourteen. Hale would never have recovered.”

Then she turns into the last pages, where it gets dark, and her finger stops. Jack knows what’s there. Thérèse at the table with the sinners, and in the margin, his pencil: *Okay, fine.* Lena’s lips move over Thérèse’s sentence. She doesn’t read that margin out.
She sets the book open on top of the dryer. She pushes up the sleeves of the Sacred Heart shirt, the left and then the right.
“*Easy*,” she says, “for *me*?”

s05d.slug: THURSDAY · 12:09 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: She has the floor, which is linoleum, and she takes all of it.

“She *couldn’t climb*. That’s the whole point of the elevator. She wasn’t some sweet little thing who never sinned and found a shortcut. She was the baby of the family, with a temper, who cried if you looked at her wrong. She had scruples so bad at twelve she was confessing things she’d only *thought about*. And she tried the stairs. She tried them every day for nine years in a convent full of women who drove her out of her mind, and she *fell down them*. Every day.” The pencil has come out of her hair, and her hair has come down, and she taps his margin with the pencil. “It was never a way for people who didn’t fall. It’s for the ones who can’t get up the stairs. You read *elevator* and you heard *cheat*.” She lowers the pencil. “It’s the only door in the building low enough for you, and you wrote *easy* on it.”
Down the row a dryer buzzes. It can buzz.

choices.text: “Augustine needed the stairs knocked out from under him. A garden in Milan. *Tolle, lege.* Little sins, little way.”
response: “Augustine needed the stairs knocked out from under him,” Jack says. “A garden in Milan, a kid singing over a wall. *Tolle, lege.* Big sins, big fall. Little sins, little way.”
“Augustine stole some pears,” Lena says, “and wrote thirteen books about it. She stole nothing and wrote one.” She shuts her eyes, serene. “His is longer because he’s a man.”

choices.text: “She cornered Leo XIII at fourteen and demanded an exception. That’s the Broussard way with a halo on it.”
response: Lena laughs out loud, bent over the book. “They had to *carry* her out,” she says. “She had both hands on the Pope’s knees and two of his guards had to pick her up off the floor.” She is enormously proud of this. “And she got in at fifteen anyway. Little never meant meek.”

choices.text: “Then it’s the only way I’d fit.”
response: “Then it’s the only way I’d fit,” he says.
Lena stops with the pencil up. She looks at him across the folding table, and the fight goes out of her face, and something gentler takes its place.
“That’s the idea,” she says.

choices.text: “Chesterton says angels can fly because they take themselves lightly. She could. Some of us can’t.”
response: “You quote Chesterton like somebody told you it counts as a sacrament,” Lena says. “She took *God* seriously. Herself, not at all. You take yourself seriously enough for a whole parish, and God like He’s the landlord.” She points the pencil at him. “You’ve got it exactly the wrong way round.”

s05e.slug: THURSDAY · 12:22 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: She takes the book back off the dryer and goes to the page she didn’t read aloud. This time she does.

She reads him Thérèse in the dark: the Easter it started, the last year and a half of her life, when heaven went shut and the thought of it stopped being sweet and turned into a fight. She reads the part about the sinners. *“She is resigned to eat the bread of sorrow as long as You desire it; she does not wish to rise up from this table filled with bitterness at which poor sinners are eating until the day set by You.”*
Then she reads his margin. “*Okay, fine*.”

She lowers the book. “You wrote that where she stops being able to feel heaven at all. Eighteen months in the dark, coughing her lungs up in an infirmary, and she says she’ll sit down at the table with the people who don’t believe a word of it and eat the bread of sorrow with them as long as He wants her there. And you wrote *okay, fine*.” She says it as if she found it carved in a pew.

choices.text: “Feeling nothing isn’t falling. She never left the table. That’s my argument, and it’s hers.”
response: “Feeling nothing isn’t falling,” Jack says. “She never left the table. That’s my argument, and it’s hers.”
“Don’t you steal my saint to win my argument.” Her eyes are very bright. She looks like she is having the time of her life being furious with him, and she isn’t trying to hide it.

choices.text: “That’s why I wrote *okay, fine*. It was the only thing I had.”
response: “That’s why I wrote *okay, fine*,” he says. “It was the only thing I had.”
She looks at the margin. She looks at him. The dryers fill the quiet, round and round.
“*Okay*,” she says, after a while. “*Fine*.” It’s his pencil, out loud in her voice, and it doesn’t sound like a shrug anymore.

choices.text: “She’d have hated Hale. Hale would’ve loved her. He’d have sent her a postcard.”
response: “He’d have sent her a postcard,” Lena says, “and she’d have prayed for him till he died of it.” She considers this with deep satisfaction. “On his deathbed. Asking for a priest. In *Latin*.”

choices.text: “You picked a saint who never had to lie to anybody.”
response: “You picked a saint who never had to lie to anybody.”
Lena goes still, and then polite. “Mr. Costigan,” she says. Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and closes on it. The dryers are very loud. He has plenty of time to hear what he said.
Then she lets go of the medal. “It’s my feast,” she says. “You’re going to apologize, and then you’re going to lose properly.”

s05f.slug: THURSDAY · 12:36 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM
body: It’s a quarter to one. She hops up and sits on the folding table among the eraser crumbs with her boots swinging, and turns to the very back of the book, past the last chapter and the letters, to the prayers the editors put at the end, and finds the one she wants by feel.

“The Act of Oblation,” she says. “Sacred Heart girls learn it at twelve.” She reads it to him, not loud: *“In the evening of this life, I shall appear before You with empty hands, for I do not ask You, Lord, to count my works.”* And a little further: *“All our justice is stained in Your eyes.”* She looks up. “All of it. Hers too. That’s the good news.”

She lets the book close on her finger. “Empty hands. That’s the little way. You don’t get to bring anything. Not your shifts, not your two pages a week, not your margins, not the books you — ” She stops herself there, carefully, and starts again lower. “You keep trying to show up with a receipt, Costigan.”
Jack looks at the padded mailer on the table, TRUMBULL in his own block capitals. A book a month. Then he looks back at her.

choices.key: At midnight on her feast Lena read you Thérèse’s ‘empty hands.’ You asked her to read it again.
response: “Read it again,” Jack says.
She does, slower, *empty hands*, *count my works*, with the dryers turning over underneath it. Nobody wins anything for a second.

choices.text: “Faith without works is dead. Saint James. Works are thank-you notes, Broussard, not receipts.”
response: “Faith without works is dead,” Jack says. “Saint James. Works are thank-you notes, Broussard, not receipts.”
“Then write one,” Lena says kindly, “and stop invoicing.”

choices.text: “I’ll show up with a pie. Gloria will rate it.”
response: “I’ll show up with a pie,” he says. “Gloria will rate it.”
“She’d give your soul a four,” Lena says. “Like the marionberry. Too much going on and not enough sugar.”

choices.text: “I’m sorry. About the lying. That was cheap, and you didn’t deserve it.”
choices.key: You apologized to Lena, on her feast, for a cheap shot.
response: “I’m sorry,” he says. “About the lying. That was cheap, and you didn’t deserve it.”
She looks at him a while over the top of the book.
“Accepted,” she says.

s05v.slug: THURSDAY · 12:44 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAUNDRY ROOM

body.text: “You still forfeit,” Lena says, and shuts the book. “House rules — even without the house.” But the corner of her mouth is back where it belongs, and when the dryer buzzes she points him at it.

“You forfeit,” Lena says, and shuts the book. “House rules — even without the house.” It’s colder than she has ever scored him. Then the dryer at the end buzzes, and she looks at it, and he watches her decide, in the set of her shoulders, that he is not going to ruin her feast. “Come on,” she says. “Fold.”

“You win,” Jack says. “On my feast?” Lena says. “Obviously.” She holds out her hand for his pencil, and he gives it to her, and she bends over the dryer with the book flat under her palm and writes under his margin, small, in his own pencil, so it will erase exactly as easily as his does.

body.title: Story of a Soul, beside the elevator

body.text: “You don’t get to win on my feast day, Costigan,” Lena says, and points straight up at the ceiling, at the pipes, at four floors of sleeping freshmen and whatever is above them. “I’m appealing to a higher court.”

Nobody wins it. Somewhere around the pie they lose the thread entirely, and by the end they’re laughing too hard to finish a sentence, and the dryer at the end of the row buzzes, and buzzes again, and nobody can get up to answer it.
“Thérèse,” Lena says, “on points.” She shuts the book on his pencil, and keeps both.

body: Then the dryers. She folds Laney’s pledge whites like a postulant, corner to corner, smoothing each one flat with the side of her hand. He folds his flannels like a dish man, fast and in thirds. When everything is done they leave both baskets on top of the dryers, side by side.
“I’m starving,” Lena says.
“Lupe’s is open till three.”

journal.title: Story of a Soul
journal.text: Thérèse of Lisieux. ICS, three dollars off the Driftwood cart, somebody’s highlighter quitting partway. My pencil: *Easy for you.* beside the elevator. *NO.* *She’d have hated Hale.* *Okay, fine.* beside the table of sinners. *Can a man and a woman be friends? Ask L.* beside her two brothers. I gave it to Lena at midnight on her feast. She wouldn’t let me erase a word. Under *Easy for you.*, with my pencil: *Empty hands. —L.* She kept it.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–one after Labor Day; she paid her Sunday. Three–one after moral luck: mine; she said I argued it like it was mine. Now four–one. Friendship: mine, arguing both sides. She said she’d never forgive me. Wednesday she said she forgives me. That was worse. Unofficial, the laundry room, midnight on her feast, no referee — the Little Way: Thérèse, on points.

s06.slug: THURSDAY · 1:02 AM · SEACLIFF ROAD, LUPE’S TRUCK
body: Out the side door, across the lot and into the Grove, where the path lamps give up and the eucalyptus at one in the morning smells of menthol and, faintly, of cat. The bark is peeling off the trunks in long strips and it cracks under their feet. The night is warm. It has been warm all week, a dry wind down off the hills that keeps the fog out at sea and makes everybody at Marisol a little reckless, and Lena walks through the Grove in her boots with the book held in both hands in front of her, all the way, as if she were carrying it up an aisle.

Lupe’s is where it always is, at the Las Olas end of Seacliff: the white truck under its string of chile lights, the radio going on the dash, and at this hour nobody in line but two surfers with wet hair and a girl in a Kappa sweatshirt eating a quesadilla through some private sorrow. Lupe leans out of the window with her gold tooth and says “Reina!” to Lena, and looks at Jack, and keeps looking. Carnitas, two. Horchata, two. They pay separately, to the penny, Lena counting quarters out of her skirt pocket.
Lupe puts the two horchatas on the counter. Then she puts a third one beside them and slides it across with one finger. “Para los novios.”
“We’re friends,” they say, both of them, at once.
“Claro,” says Lupe, and shows them the tooth.

On the radio Vicente Fernández wants to go back to somebody, and says so, and says so again. They eat on two of Lupe’s milk crates beside the truck with the paper boats on their knees, and the third horchata sits on the asphalt at their feet, sweating, unclaimed. Lena eats one-handed with the book open on her knee. She is reading his margins as she goes, every one, and he knows exactly where the last one is.
She gets there. The part near the end where Thérèse writes about the two missionary priests she was given to pray for, her brothers.

body.title: Story of a Soul, beside the brothers
body.text: *Can a man and a woman be friends? Ask L.*

body: Lena reads it. She looks up at him over the paper boat.
“Ask me what?”

choices.text: “Whether it counts. A man and a woman. By letters.”
choices.key: At Lupe’s, Lena found your margin — *Ask L.* You told her you wanted to know if it counts: a man and a woman, by letters.
response: “Whether it counts,” he says. “A man and a woman. By letters.”

“It counted for her.” Lena turns back a page, to the two priests. “She called them her brothers and she meant it. She met one of them once, through a grille, for an afternoon. The other one, never.” She shuts the book on her finger and stands up. “Shipwreck Cove is two streets over,” she says. “I’ve never seen it.”
“Whether you’d have written back.”
“Every day,” Lena says. “With citations.” She folds her paper boat into quarters, very precisely, and stands up with the book. “Shipwreck Cove is two streets over,” she says. “I’ve never seen it.”
“I forget.”

“No you don’t,” Lena says, mildly, and lets him keep the lie, like a cookie he stole off the counter. She brushes tortilla off her skirt and stands up with the book. “Shipwreck Cove is two streets over,” she says. “I’ve never seen it.”

body: Del Playa ends at the bluff in a turnaround and a sign about hours nobody keeps, and then the wooden stairs go down: switchback after switchback of warped gray boards sanded soft by thirty years of bare feet, somebody’s Christmas lights still stapled along the rail and plugged into nothing. Lena goes first. Laney has told her about the bonfires down here. Jack has never come. The first night of all, he walked the other way.
Nobody tonight. A cold fire ring of black rocks, a melted Solo cup, a flip-flop.

The tide is out, far out, and the sand it left is hard and wet and shining, and standing up out of it near the foot of the bluff are the ribs of the schooner: black timbers curving up from the beach in two ragged rows, the bones of a boat nobody alive remembers going down. Past them the moon, three nights short of full, hangs over the water to the southwest, toward the Point, and it has laid a road of light across the whole Pacific to their feet.

It’s warm. There’s no fog anywhere. Lena stands in the wet sand in her boots and reads Thérèse to him by moonlight, and where the moon isn’t enough, by the green glow of the LG held open over the page. He sits on a rib of the ship. She reads the part where Thérèse wants to be everything at once — warrior, priest, apostle, martyr — and goes looking through Saint Paul for her place in the body, and can’t find it, and then does. *“O Jesus, my Love… my vocation, at last I have found it… MY VOCATION IS LOVE!”* Lena does the French where she has it from the nuns, *ma vocation, c’est l’Amour*, in a New Orleans accent that is mostly vowels and entirely sure of itself. Once, mid-page, she looks up at the scar through his eyebrow, and doesn’t ask.

Then she closes the book on the phone and opens the phone instead and thumbs through it, frowning, the screen lighting her chin. She finds what she wants. “Harry Choates,” she says. “1946. ‘Jolie Blonde.’ The Cajun national anthem. Every wedding in Breaux Bridge. My Mémère’s from Breaux Bridge.”
Out of the little speaker it’s tinny and sweet and sawing: a dead man’s fiddle, a dead man’s voice crying something in French, on a beach in California at a quarter to two in the morning.
“It’s a waltz,” Lena says. “Get up. I’ll teach you.”

choices.key: At Shipwreck Cove Lena taught you the Cajun waltz to “Jolie Blonde.”
response: He gets up off the ship. She props the LG against a rib with the speaker facing up, and takes his left hand in her right, and puts his other hand at her back, and sets her free hand on his shoulder.
“*Un*, *deux*, *trois*,” she says. “Long, short, short. Don’t bounce. Cajuns don’t bounce.”

He bounces. He steps on her boot. She says something in French that he is fairly sure is not in the Act of Oblation. Then, somehow, on the hard sand by the ribs, they have it: the slow turn and the three-count, round the cold fire ring and back, the fiddle sawing away under the timbers.

Her back is warm under his palm through the thin cotton, and her hair is all the way down, and she is laughing at his feet with her face turned up close to his; and he wants her, the whole of her, here, on this beach, and all of what it costs is in his right hand, which has to stay exactly where it is at the small of her back and not draw her the last little way in, and does stay, every bar, to the end of the song.
The song ends. Lena steps back first. “Not bad,” she says, “for a man who bounces,” and goes to get the phone.
“I’ll watch,” he says.
“Your loss,” says Lena, and dances it anyway.

She dances it alone, in her boots, on the hard wet sand by the bones of the ship, to a fiddler dead sixty years: the slow turn, the long step and the two short ones, one arm up around a partner who isn’t there and the other out to the side, holding the hem of her skirt. She isn’t good at it. She is wonderful at it. She shuts her eyes for the last verse and nearly waltzes into the fire ring, and laughs at the dark, and keeps going.

He wants her. He sits on the ship with both hands on the wet wood and wants her — the boots, the bad turns, the hair coming down, the laugh she gives the dark when she misses a step, the whole bright stubborn rest of her. He watches every bar. He will never get it out of his head, and he lets it in.

choices.key: At Shipwreck Cove you lit a cigarette on her feast day. Reliquary No. 5.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. No. 5: Shipwreck Cove, on her feast day. ‘Really.’

response: He gets the Reds out of his jeans, and the lighter, and cups it, and the flame is very loud and very orange in all that dark.

Lena stops the song. She crosses the sand in her boots and takes the cigarette out of his mouth and pinches it out between her thumb and finger, hissing at the heat. Out of the top of her left boot comes the Altoids tin. She tears a strip off the paper boat from Lupe’s, which she has kept for no reason until now, and writes on her knee with a ballpoint.

response.title: In the tin
response.text: No. 5 · 10/1/09 · Shipwreck Cove · on my feast day, Costigan, really.

response: She snaps the lid shut on it. Then she starts the song over and dances it alone anyway, slow, in her boots, by the ribs of the ship, and he watches her with the one drag still in his mouth.

s06c.slug: THURSDAY · 2:04 AM · SHIPWRECK COVE, THE WATERLINE
body: After a while they walk down to the water. The wash slides up the sand in thin sheets and slides back, and Lena stands just where it reaches the toes of her boots and then doesn’t. The moon is lower now, over toward the Point, and the road it lays down is shorter.

She tries to let the Pacific touch her boots and steps back every time it does. She wants to know where Ohio keeps its ocean. He tells her Lake Erie. “That’s a puddle with a Coast Guard,” Lena says. He tells her Lake Erie died once, in the seventies, officially, in the newspapers, and they brought it back. She considers this with her head on one side. “Lazarus Erie,” she says, and he laughs, and she looks very pleased with herself, and the wash comes up and she steps back.

body.text: There’s sand on her boots from the waltz, up to the stitching.
He can still taste the one drag.

body: “Do you know what you’re doing yet?” she asks.
She asks it lightly, the way she’d ask a witness the one question she has been saving all night.

He starts to answer. He has something — the outline of something: Friday, the bleachers, the First Way coming back to him word for word out of a girl’s mouth, the red truck in the fire lane, *she’s* — and it isn’t there. He reaches for the next part, and there is no next part.
“No,” he says. “I don’t know, Lena.”
Down the beach a wave folds over and hisses up the sand. Then, because the quiet is worse than anything he could put in it: “She’s so nice. She’s — sweet.”

The laugh gets out of Lena before she can stop it. Loud and startled, out it comes, and her hand flies up to her mouth too late to catch any of it, and she turns half away with her hand still there and her shoulders going.
“Come up with a better answer before somebody else asks you, Youngstown,” she says, when she can. “That is the worst thing you can say about a person in this situation.”

And he sees it. He sees it cross her, quicker than she can cover it. Her shoulders come down from wherever they’ve been all month. She looks at the water, too fast. Her hand finds his sleeve and holds on, and lets go. Something in her face says she knows exactly what just went across it, and wishes he’d been looking at the ocean.

body.text: The LG in her other hand has lit up with the time, 2:04, and all at once Jack remembers that Becca said she would pray for two in the morning: a girl in Portolá with a rosary in the dark, praying for him. Now.

choices.key: At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You told her she looked relieved. She said she wasn’t.
response: “You look relieved,” he says.

“I’m not relieved.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and holds it there. She says it straight to him, and then she goes back to the water, and the wash comes up over the toes of her boots and she lets it.

response: “You look relieved,” he says.

“I’m not relieved.” Her hand goes to the medal at her throat and holds it there. She says it straight to him, and then she goes back to the water, and the wash comes up over the toes of her boots and she lets it.

choices.key: At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You asked her what the right answer was.
response: “Then what’s the right answer?”

She thinks about it. She actually thinks about it, with the wash at her boots — she thinks about everything he asks her, which is part of the trouble. “There isn’t one at two in the morning on a beach,” Lena says. “Ask me in daylight.”

choices.text: Let her have it. Look at the water.
choices.key: At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You let her have it and looked at the water.
response: He looks at the water. It goes on being enormous and black and silver at the edges and entirely uninterested in either of them.
After a while, so does she. Properly, this time.

choices.key: At the waterline Lena asked if you knew what you were doing. You said Becca’s nice. She laughed. You said you’d workshop it.
response: “I’ll workshop it.”
“Workshop it with Gloria,” Lena says. “She’ll rate it.” She considers. “She’ll give it a two. Store-bought crust.”

s06d.slug: THURSDAY · 3:58 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY
body: They stayed on the ribs of the ship until the cold came up off the sand, a little after three, and didn’t say much. When they got up to go, he said that if you walked to the far end of the cove, around the rocks, you could see the old light on the Point from underneath. Lena said no. She didn’t say why. She started back the other way, for the stairs, and he went after her. Up Del Playa, through Las Olas with its porch lights off, through the Grove, not touching.

The lobby at 3:58 is all fluorescent hum and the smell of the carpet. Marcus is asleep at the front desk on his forearms, a highlighter uncapped in one fist and the orgo open under his cheek. The Fishbowl TV is still on with the sound off, a man selling knives to the empty couches.
“Our laundry,” Lena says. “It’s still on the dryers.”
Neither of them goes down for it.
She presses the button. The elevator comes down slow from somewhere and opens on its own empty light, and she stands in front of it with the book against her chest and doesn’t get in.
“That was a terrible thing to be glad about,” she says.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. Tuesday he called on the dot, from his room. He’s bought a ticket for Columbus Day weekend; wants to see the Pacific. She told him it’s a threat. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’

choices.key: At the Delgado elevator, at four in the morning, Lena said it was a terrible thing to be glad about. You said: me too.
response: “I know,” Jack says. “Me too.”
“Don’t.” She steps into the elevator. “Don’t agree with me at four in the morning.”
The doors come together on her and the book, and the light over them climbs to 2 and stops.

choices.key: At the Delgado elevator Lena said it was a terrible thing to be glad about. You wished her a happy feast day.
response: “Happy feast day, Lena.”
She nearly smiles. “It’s been a very good one,” she says. “That’s the trouble.”
She gets in. The doors take their time, and the last of her he sees is the toe of one boot.

choices.key: At four in the morning you walked Lena up the stairs. At the second floor she sent you to bed.
response: He lets the elevator close on nobody and pushes open the door to the east stairwell, and she comes. Their steps are very loud in it, boots and sneakers on concrete, sand grinding under both, all the way up to the second-floor door.
She stops with her hand on the bar. “Go to bed, Jack.”
He goes on up first. Half a flight later he hears the door below open, and shut.

choices.key: At the Delgado elevator Lena said it was a terrible thing to be glad about. You let the elevator take her.
response: He lets it.

She steps in and turns around with the book held against her, and they look at each other across the lobby carpet while the doors make up their minds, and then the doors come together, and then she isn’t there.
